The most common cause of hyperphosphatemia is acute or chronic renal disease. In normal conditions, the kidney of healthy
individuals has the capacity to excrete about 67% of their absorbed phosphate via the urine. However, when there is a decline in
kidney function, the homeostasis of phosphorus is altered, and this occurs even at the early stages of kidney disease (Stremke and
Gallant, 2018). Kidney disease is a progressive disease where glomerular ﬁltration rate (GFR) is reduced, and phosphorus cannot be
excreted, causing an increase in serum phosphorus concentration. In early renal disease, PTH secretions increase to maintain normal
phosphorus concentrations, and though PTH concentrations are elevated, they remain within the upper limits of the normal range.
